The '''1973–74 season''' was the 75th completed season of [[The Football League]].

[[Don Revie]] marked his last season as [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]]'s manager by guiding them to league championship glory, before taking over from [[Alf Ramsey|Sir Alf Ramsey]] as the [[England national football team]] manager, with [[England national football team|England]] having failed to qualify for the [[1974 FIFA World Cup|1974 World Cup]]. Revie's conquering side had a two-horse race with [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] all season but won in the end, taking the title for the second time in their history by five points. Newly promoted [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] adapted well to life back in the top flight, finishing in sixth place.

[[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] were relegated from the [[Football League First Division|First Division]] just six years after winning the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] at the end of a traumatic season. Their 36-year stay at the top was finally ended by a 1–0 home defeat against [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]]. Former United striker [[Denis Law]] scored City's winning goal. But [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]]'s win on that same afternoon would have sent United down even if they had beaten City. Despite this the board kept faith in manager [[Tommy Docherty]] as the man to regain the club's top flight place.

Joining United in the [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] were [[Norwich City F.C.|Norwich City]] and [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]]. This was the first season in which the League introduced three relegation places from the top division.

Former Leeds player [[Jack Charlton]] had a fine debut in management by guiding [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]] to the Second Division title and a place in the First Division. Second in the table were [[Luton Town F.C.|Luton Town]], who finished 15 points behind the runaway champions. Third-placed [[Carlisle United F.C.|Carlisle United]], managed by Alan Ashman (who won the FA Cup with West Bromwich Albion in 1968), gained a place in the First Division for the first, and so far only, time in their history, completing a rapid rise from the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] to the First Division. [[Crystal Palace F.C.|Crystal Palace]], [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]] and [[Swindon Town F.C.|Swindon Town]] were all relegated.

Promotion from the Third Division was secured by champions [[Oldham Athletic A.F.C.|Oldham Athletic]], [[Bristol Rovers F.C.|Bristol Rovers]] and [[York City F.C.|York City]], which at the time represented York's highest ever League finish. [[Cambridge United F.C.|Cambridge United]], [[Shrewsbury Town F.C.|Shrewsbury Town]], [[Southport F.C.|Southport]] and [[Rochdale A.F.C.|Rochdale]] were all relegated.

[[Peterborough United F.C.|Peterborough United]] won Division Four and were promoted along with [[Gillingham F.C.|Gillingham]], [[Colchester United F.C.|Colchester United]] and [[Bury F.C.|Bury]]. The league's re-election system voted in favour of the bottom four league clubs and there were no departures or arrivals in the league in 1974.

==Final league tables and results==

The tables below are reproduced here in the exact form that they can be found at [https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1973-74.html The Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation] website<ref name="rsssf">{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1973-74.html |title=England 1973–74 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=2010-02-24| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100127134350/http://www.rsssf.com/engpaul/FLA/1973-74.html| archive-date= 27 January 2010 <!--DASHBot-->| url-status= live}}</ref> and in ''Rothmans Book of Football League Records 1888–89 to 1978–79'',<ref name="Rothmans">Ian Laschke: ''Rothmans Book of Football League Records 1888–89 to 1978–79''. Macdonald and Jane’s, London & Sydney, 1980.</ref> with home and away statistics separated.

Beginning with the season 1894–95, clubs finishing level on points were separated according to goal average (goals scored divided by goals conceded), or more properly put, goal ratio. In case one or more teams had the same goal difference, this system favoured those teams who had scored fewer goals. The goal average system was eventually scrapped beginning with the 1976–77 season. 

This season marked the introduction of [[Promotion and relegation|relegating]] the bottom three teams in the league, replacing the previous system in which only the bottom two were relegated, in place since automatic promotion/relegation was introduced in the [[1898–99 Football League|1898-99 season]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://efl.com/about-the-efl/history/innovation|title=Innovation|website=Efl.com|access-date=June 26, 2026}}</ref> Since the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] was established in the [[1958–59 Football League|1958–59 season]], the bottom four teams of that division have been required to apply for [[re-election (Football League)|re-election]].<ref name="Rothmans"/>

'''Match results''' are drawn from ''Rothmans'' for all divisions.<ref name="Rothmans"/>

1973 - 74 was the final season for the long-serving managers of two of the First Division's leading clubs. Both are regarded as having transformed their clubs on and off the field during lengthy reigns lasting more than a decade. [[Don Revie]] guided Leeds United to the title before calling time of 13 years as manager at [[Elland Road]] to take charge of the [[England national football team|England team]]. [[Bill Shankly]] announced his retirement as [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] manager after 15 years after they finished second in the league and triumphed 3–0 over [[Newcastle United]] in the [[1974 FA Cup Final|FA Cup Final]].

Despite the controversial resignation of manager [[Brian Clough]] in October, [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] finished third after their former player [[Dave Mackay]] returned to the [[Baseball Ground]] as Clough's successor. [[Ipswich Town F.C.|Ipswich Town]] continued to thrive among the First Division's leading company by finishing fourth in their fifth campaign under [[Bobby Robson]]. [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke City]] enjoyed another strong season, finishing fifth, with England goalkeeper [[Peter Shilton]] keeping opposition strikers at bay after his predecessor [[Gordon Banks]] retired due to an eye injury suffered in a car crash. [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] enjoyed a strong return to the First Division after two seasons away by finishing sixth.

[[Manchester United]]'s 36-year spell in the First Division ended in relegation, while their cross-city rivals finished 14th and were beaten in the [[Football League Cup]] final by [[Wolverhampton Wanderers]]. [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]]'s eight-year spell in the First Division ended in relegation despite 21 goals from the division's top scorer [[Mick Channon]] and a change of manager from [[Ted Bates (footballer)|Ted Bates]] to [[Lawrie McMenemy]] before Christmas. [[Norwich City F.C.|Norwich City]]'s second season among the elite ended in relegation.

[[Jack Charlton]] started his managerial career by guiding [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]] to the Second Division title and a place in the First Division. Middlesbrough finished 15 points above runners-up [[Luton Town F.C.|Luton Town]], who ended their 14-year exile from the elite despite financial difficulties. The final promotion place was snatched by [[Carlisle United]], who reached the First Division for the first time in their history. [[Leyton Orient F.C.|Orient]] missed out on promotion by a single point. Other teams who just missed out on promotion included [[Nottingham Forest]], 
[[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] and [[West Bromwich Albion]].

Crystal Palace were relegated for a second successive season, while Preston North End went down in their first season under the management of the legendary [[Bobby Charlton]], who then re-registered himself as a player in his efforts to reverse the decline of the once great [[Lancashire]] club. Swindon Town went down in bottom place after five seasons in the Second Division.
